claims.text: HEA nanoparticle premelting and melting behavior is predominantly governed by the interplay of high configurational entropy and strong nanoparticle–support anchoring.
High configurational entropy retards phase segregation in HEA nanoparticles.
Strong support anchoring increases the energy barrier for surface atomic diffusion.
Strong support anchoring suppresses nanoparticle coalescence.
Support anchoring elevates the onset temperatures of premelting and melting relative to unsupported nanoparticles.
Defective turbostratic graphite provides numerous nanoparticle nucleation sites.
Nanoparticles can partially intercalate and take root at graphite edge planes, producing high binding energy and strong anchoring.
Nanoparticle–support interfacial bonding modifies nanoparticle surface energy.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the mixed elemental phase of HEA nanoparticles at the nanoscale.
Strong chemical and physical interactions with a support increase the effective melting temperature by inhibiting surface diffusion and premature coalescence.
Free-standing HEA nanoparticles exhibit earlier premelting and greater surface diffusion than strongly supported particles.
Free-standing HEA nanoparticles are more prone to elemental segregation than strongly supported particles.
Supported HEA nanoparticles will retain their size and morphology to higher temperatures than composition- and size-matched free-standing nanoparticles.
Supported HEA nanoparticles will have a higher premelting or melting onset temperature than matched free-standing nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles strongly anchored on carbon supports can retain excellent thermal stability during annealing up to 1173 K.
The proposed support-governed behavior should hold for sub-10 nm nanoparticles over approximately 500–1200 K.
The proposed behavior may deviate for significantly larger particles or under oxidizing conditions.
